meta.name: How to Find a Responsible Dog Breeder (and Verify What They Tell You)
meta.title_tag: How to Find a Reputable Dog Breeder & What to Ask
meta.excerpt: A responsible breeder health-tests both parents and lets you check the results yourself, lets you meet the mother where the puppies are raised, asks you as many questions as you ask them, and puts a return-to-breeder promise in writing. Here's where to find one, what to ask, how to verify OFA results, and the answers that should make you walk away.
meta.meta_description: Where to find a reputable dog breeder, what to ask, how to check OFA health tests yourself, and what a fair contract, deposit and guarantee look like.
meta.author: Kailun Zhang

hero.alt: Golden Retriever mother with her seven-week-old litter in a clean home setting — what meeting the parents at a responsible breeder looks like

body_html:
Quick Answer: Start with your breed's national parent club or your vet, not a classified ad or a pet store. A responsible breeder health-tests both parents and gives you their registered names so you can look up the results yourself on ofa.org. They let you meet the mother where the puppies are raised, ask you as many questions as you ask them, and put a return-to-breeder clause in a written contract. How to check health tests ↓

Where to Look for a Breeder, and Where Not To

The American Kennel Club doesn't license, endorse or recommend specific breeders. It points buyers to each breed's national "parent club," which has a breeder-referral contact (AKC).

  • Good places to start: the parent club's contact (via AKC's breeder referral search), your vet, owners of the breed, and dog shows (OFA; Humane World for Animals, formerly the Humane Society of the United States).
  • AKC Marketplace, with caveats. It's a listing service. Its site disclaimer says AKC doesn't sell dogs, makes no guarantee about a dog's health, quality or parentage, and isn't responsible for sales made there. Badges such as Breeder of Merit appear on Marketplace listings, but AKC says it doesn't distribute badges to breeders, so a badge graphic on a seller's own website isn't proof; look the breeder up in AKC's Breeder of Merit participant search instead. Breeder of Merit requires parent-club health testing, but at the basic level the breeder certifies it themselves (AKC), so check OFA anyway.
  • Places to skip: pet stores, brokers and ship-only sellers. Humane World says a responsible breeder won't sell in any way that prevents meeting and interviewing you.

Responsible Breeder vs. Red Flags at a Glance

What to checkResponsible breederRed flag
Health testingParents screened for the breed's recommended tests; names shared so you can verify (OFA)"Vet-checked" only, or results you can't find on ofa.org (OFA)
The motherWith her puppies; the father often lives elsewhere (AKC)Mother "not available"; handoff in a parking lot
Where puppies liveIn the home, around people and everyday noise (OFA)Won't show you where the litter is raised
Questions for youAbout your household, schedule, past dogs and training plans (AKC)First question is how soon you can pay a deposit (AKC)
Go-home age8 weeks or older; toy breeds often up to 12 weeks (AKC)Puppies offered before 8 weeks
ContractWritten, with a return-to-breeder clause (AKC, OFA)No contract, or none you can read before paying
AvailabilityOften a waiting list (OFA)Many breeds, puppies always ready, "teacup" sizes (Humane World, AKC)

A breeder who passes most of these checks but won't share health results hasn't passed.

How to Verify Health Testing Yourself

"Vet-checked" means a vet examined the puppy. Health testing means the parents were screened for inherited problems before breeding. Young puppies can't be screened for hip dysplasia, so OFA says to review the parents' and grandparents' results.

  1. Find your breed's list. OFA's browse-by-breed page shows the screenings each parent club recommends for breeding dogs.
  2. Get both parents' registered names or registration numbers, not call names. OFA warns against results you can't verify.
  3. Search OFA's database by registered name, registration number or OFA/CHIC number. Confirm each result is the right dog and current; the Golden Retriever Club of America treats eye exams as valid for 12 months.
  4. Read the result. In an OFA number such as LR-100E24M-C-PI, "E" is the grade (Excellent) and "24" the age in months at testing. Excellent, Good and Fair hips are normal, Borderline is unclear, and Mild, Moderate and Severe are dysplastic. Final hip and elbow certification requires age 24 months or older (OFA).
  5. Know what CHIC means. A CHIC number means the dog completed every recommended test and the results are public, not that every result was normal (OFA). Open each one.

Abnormal hip and elbow results appear only if the owner allows it (OFA), so ask for the paper report if something is missing. A DNA "carrier" result isn't automatically a problem: AKC explains that breeding a carrier to a clear dog won't produce puppies affected by a recessive condition.

What the lists look like (OFA, checked September 2026):

  • Cavalier King Charles Spaniel: hips (OFA or PennHIP), an eye exam by a board-certified ophthalmologist, patellas (kneecaps), and a board-certified cardiologist's heart exam, recommended yearly.
  • French Bulldog: hips, eyes, patellas and cardiac, with the RFGS breathing exam optional. RFGS grades 0 and I mean clinically unaffected. Ask for it anyway; our brachycephalic buyer guide explains why.
  • Labrador Retriever: hips, elbows, eyes, and DNA tests for exercise-induced collapse and the dilute gene.
  • Golden Retriever: the breed club asks for hips and elbows plus a yearly ophthalmologist exam and a cardiologist's heart exam after 12 months (GRCA).

Most doodle crosses, including Goldendoodles and Cavapoos, have no CHIC list of their own (the Australian Labradoodle, registered through its breed associations, is the exception), so ask for each parent breed's tests; see our doodle breeding guide. PennHIP, an alternative hip method, can be done from 16 weeks (Antech).

Questions to Ask a Dog Breeder, and Answers That Should Worry You

OFA's advice: if a breeder has no answer or hesitates too long, reconsider.

  • "What health problems does this breed have, and what were the parents tested for?" Worry about "my dogs have never had problems."
  • "Can I meet the mother? Who is the father?" The father may belong to another breeder, but his records should be available (OFA).
  • "Why did you breed this litter?" OFA says "to sell" isn't enough.
  • "Can I read the contract before I pay anything?" Worry about "after the deposit."
  • "Can I contact you after pickup?" AKC says a good breeder stays a resource for the dog's life.
  • "Will I get the AKC registration application at pickup?" AKC warns against "AKC hasn't sent the papers yet" excuses and look-alike registries, and says "papers" and AKC registration aren't the same thing. If the application isn't ready at pickup, AKC advises waiting to pay until it is.

Questions a Good Breeder Will Ask You

Expect to be interviewed about your previous dogs, who lives with you, your work schedule, where the puppy will live and how you'll train it (AKC). OFA says a responsible breeder asks as many questions as you do, and a waiting list is normal. Being screened isn't proof on its own: BBB says scam sellers often fake a screening process to look legitimate, so pair it with the health-test and visit checks.

The Visit: Meeting the Mother and the Puppies

Humane World says to always visit where the puppy was born and raised. AKC notes first introductions sometimes happen over video; on a live call, ask to see the mother, the litter and the room. That's a first step, not a substitute: BBB's 2025 puppy-scam update describes one scammer using AI-generated video, though it says such cases are still limited. Can't visit before paying the balance? Read our puppy scams guide first.

In person, look for a clean space, lively puppies and a relaxed mother with them (AKC), and adult dogs that are friendly rather than fearful with the breeder (OFA).

Contracts, Deposits and Health Guarantees

According to AKC's guide to breeder contracts (June 2025), they usually include:

  • The basics: the puppy's and parents' registration numbers and the price.
  • Limited registration for pet puppies: AKC events except dog shows are open to the dog, but its puppies can't be registered.
  • Spay/neuter terms, sometimes delayed until growth plates close. Check the timing with your vet first.
  • Return-to-breeder clause: at any age, for any reason, the dog goes back to the breeder, or, at minimum, the breeder is notified of any change of ownership.
  • Health guarantee: genetic defects up to a set age, or specific conditions, sometimes with conditions for you.

Before signing, ask what the guarantee requires of you, what the remedy is, and whether it means returning the dog. Get deposit terms in writing before paying, and use a credit card if you have one (FTC).

This isn't legal advice. As of 2023, 22 states had "puppy lemon laws," which typically apply only to pet stores, though some, like California's, also cover breeders (Michigan State University's Animal Legal & Historical Center). Your state consumer protection office can tell you what applies.

Puppy Mills, Pet Stores and What "USDA-Licensed" Means

The ASPCA says pet stores often buy from brokers who buy puppies in bulk from commercial breeders, so a store can't really vouch for a puppy's source. Pet-store puppies can come with AKC papers too (AKC inspects pet stores' records), so papers don't point to a responsible breeder.

A USDA license is generally needed for wholesale sales and for retail sales where the buyer can't see the dog before buying. Face-to-face sales are exempt, as are breeders with four or fewer breeding females selling only puppies they raised (USDA APHIS, November 2018). A license means minimum standards apply, not quality. Humane World's April 2026 "Horrible Hundred" report, a selection of 100 problem breeders and sellers drawn from state and USDA inspection records, found more than half were USDA-licensed. It's a selected list, not a random sample.

What a Fair Price Reflects

OFA says a good breeder will likely charge at the high end of the range, and that this isn't the time to hunt for a bargain. OFA's registry fees alone (in effect since January 2022) are $45 for hips ($50 with elbows) and $15 each for an eye, cardiac, patella, thyroid or DNA result, or $10 each when three or more soft-tissue results, such as eye, cardiac and patella, are submitted together for one dog. Vet, specialist and lab fees are extra, and eye and heart exams are often repeated. For one Cavalier parent, OFA's fees for hips, eyes, patellas and cardiac come to $75–$90 before any vet bill.

Our cost guides estimate a health-tested puppy at $1,500–$3,500 for a Cavalier, $2,500–$5,000+ for a French Bulldog, $2,000–$5,000 for a Goldendoodle and $2,000–$4,500 for a Cavapoo. These are our estimates, not survey data.

Price alone proves nothing either way. You're paying for testing, so verify it.

Breeder Vetting Checklist

  • Checked your breed's recommended tests on OFA.
  • Found both parents' current results on ofa.org.
  • Met the mother where the litter is raised.
  • Answered the breeder's questions about your home.
  • Read the contract, guarantee and deposit terms before paying.
  • Paying by a method with buyer protection.
  • Puppy at least 8 weeks at pickup, with vet records.
  • First vet visit booked within the guarantee window.

Written by Kailun Zhang, who is not a veterinarian, breeder or lawyer. This guide summarizes the sources below and isn't legal or veterinary advice; rules vary by state.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the signs of a responsible dog breeder?

They health-test both parents for their breed's recommended screenings, with results you can check on ofa.org, and keep the mother with puppies raised in the home. They interview you, send puppies home at 8 weeks or older, and use a written contract with a return-to-breeder clause (AKC, OFA).

What questions should I ask a dog breeder?

Ask what the parents were tested for and their registered names, whether you can meet the mother, how the puppies are raised and what the contract covers. Reconsider a breeder who can't answer (OFA).

How do I check whether a breeder's health testing is real?

Search both parents' registered names or OFA numbers on ofa.org and compare the results with your breed's recommended tests. OFA says its certifications can all be verified online and to beware of results you can't verify.

Does AKC registration mean a puppy is healthy or well-bred?

No. AKC says registration doesn't guarantee health or quality, and it doesn't license or endorse breeders. For health, check the parents' results on OFA.

Is a non-refundable puppy deposit normal?

There's no standard rule. Get the terms in writing before paying: the amount, whether it's refundable, and what happens if no suitable puppy is born. Pay by credit card if you have one; the FTC says no legitimate seller will require gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency. If a seller you haven't met asks for more money after the deposit, for shipping, a crate or insurance, stop paying, contact your bank or card issuer, and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Is a USDA-licensed breeder a good breeder?

Not necessarily. A USDA license mostly applies to breeders who sell wholesale or sight unseen, and it sets minimum standards, not quality. More than half of the breeders in Humane World's 2026 Horrible Hundred report, a list of 100 problem sellers, were USDA-licensed.
